name: Scots
about: Scots is English's sister, not its slang: both grew out of Old English, and Scots was the tongue of the Scottish court and its laws for centuries.
About 1.5 million people told the 2011 census they could speak it, from Glasgow and the Borders to the Doric of the North East.
Orkney and Shetland speak it too, salted with Norn, the Norse tongue the islands spoke before Scots arrived.
The Scottish Languages Act 2025 gave Scots official status in Scotland, alongside Gaelic.

lessons.title: Aye, naw and hullo
intro: Sit doon, pet. Scots isnae bad English, it's a language wi its ain words.
Ye'll hear maist o these afore ye've finished yer scone.

words.note: Rhymes with 'jaw'. You'll also hear 'na' and 'no'.
A wee dram, a wee minute, a wee bit dreich.
You'll see it on signs as you leave a town.

words.english: Dull, grey and damp (of the weather)
words.note: Throaty 'ch', like 'loch'. Scotland's favourite word for most days.

lessons.tip: Scots spelling isn't fixed: 'Hoo's it gaun', 'How's it gaun' and 'Hou's it gaun' are all fair. Say it and folk will understand.

lessons.title: Fit like? The Doric
intro: Up here we spik the Doric, the Scots o the North East.
Swap yer 'wh' for an 'f' and ye're halfway there, loon.

words.note: Literally 'what like?'. The answer is 'Nae bad'.
In Ulster Scots 'fit' means foot. Mind which side o the water ye're on.
'Far are ye gaun?' Where are you going?
Further south it's 'dinnae'.

lessons.tip: Doric turns 'wh' into 'f': fit (what), far (where), fa (who), fan (when). The local joke: 'Furry boots are ye fae?' is 'Whereabouts are you from?'

lessons.title: Rabbie Burns
intro: Robert Burns, born in Alloway in 1759, wrote in Scots and the world still sings him.
Every 25 January there's a Burns Supper somewhere, wi haggis, whisky and far too many speeches.

words.note: 'Syne' rhymes with 'sign', not 'zine'. Sung at midnight on Hogmanay the world over.
From Auld Lang Syne: 'we'll tak a cup o kindness yet'.
To a Mouse opens 'Wee, sleekit, cow'rin, tim'rous beastie'.
'The best laid schemes o mice an men gang aft agley': often go wrong. Also To a Mouse.
Burns's praise of the haggis, in Address to a Haggis.

words.local: A man's a man for a' that
words.english: People are equal, whatever their rank
words.say: a MANZ a MAN for AW that
words.note: Sung at the opening of the Scottish Parliament in 1999.

lessons.tip: Burns's first book, the Kilmarnock edition of 1786, was called Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect. It sold out.

lessons.title: Peerie words: Shetland and Orkney
intro: Wir dialect is Scots, but the Vikings left their words in it.
Norn was spoken here once. Hit's gone, but no all o hit.

words.note: Shetland's 'wee'.
Orkney's 'wee'. Get them the wrong way round at your peril.
Shetland kept the old 'thou'. You'd say 'you' to a stranger.
From Old Norse. Sullom Voe, Olna Voe.
In June it never gets properly dark this far north.
Rhymes with 'cow'. Trows live in the hills and love fiddle music.

words.english: The old Norse tongue of the isles

lessons.tip: Lerwick's fire festival, Up Helly Aa, burns a Viking galley every January.
